candidates.title: CoSA: The Conflict of Skills Attack in Real-World LLM Agent Ecosystems
candidates.institution: 9 authors incl. affiliation with Institute of Computing Technology (per Semantic Scholar); full author list: Yujia Zheng, Tianhao Li, Shangzhi Xu et al.
communitySignals: Picked up by Korean community arxiv-trend aggregator (roomedia/ax-trend #3583, 2026-10-28)
no Papers with Code entry located
credibilityEvidence: Full text read: formalizes Conflict of Skills (CoS) via controlled executions of real public Agent Skills with matched single-Skill controls, identifies 4 recurring composition mechanisms
CoSA-Bench: 288 tasks across recruiting/finance/IT/business domains; across 5 LLMs and 3 agent harnesses, additions capped at 5% of each pool raise policy-violation rate 35.02%->58.45% (+23.43pp)
Defense: a lightweight harness-level guard checking information flow/authorization drops violations from 65.28% to 6.67% on OpenClaw recruiting tasks, with reported benign-task completion tradeoff
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Mechanism identification + benchmark + working defense with before/after numbers across multiple LLMs and harnesses; a genuinely new compositional-risk framing distinct from single-skill auditing
reproducibilityEvidence: Official code repository SIGMIR-ORG/CoSA on GitHub
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Well-specified attack taxonomy, benchmark construction and defense all back a narrow, clearly-bounded claim (skill composition can defeat per-skill vetting)
candidates.primaryLimitation: Evaluated via controlled/benchmark executions rather than live production marketplaces; generalization to arbitrary real-world Skill ecosystems beyond CoSA-Bench's 4 domains is not established
candidates.presentationReason: Attack mechanism, benchmark construction and defense are all precisely specified with numeric results
candidates.reason: Selected: identifies a genuinely new agent-ecosystem attack surface (safe skills composing into unsafe behavior) with a working benchmark and defense; previously held in watch pool (2026-10-28) only because that day's slot went to a different cluster, not for any credibility gap.

candidates.title: Where You Inject Matters: The Trust Region Effect in LLM Agents
candidates.citationVelocity: published 3 days; Semantic Scholar 429 rate-limited on 2 retries, not individually confirmed but recency makes 0 citations near-certain
candidates.institution: University of Chicago, Microsoft Research, University of Rochester, Simon Fraser University, UC Davis, UIUC (10 authors incl. Bo Li, Jianfeng Gao)
communitySignals: Summarized by community arxiv-digest bot (matouskozak/arxiv-digest issue #259, 2026-10-30)
not found in HF Daily Papers batches checked
no Papers with Code repo located
credibilityEvidence: Full text read: 3 agentic testbeds (coding on Terminal-Bench-2, tool-use on AgentDojo, workflow on DecodingTrust-Agent), 36 environmental surfaces, 8 victim agents (GPT-5.6/5.4/5-mini/4o, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Grok-4.6, Opus5, Sonnet5)
Deterministic script-based verifiers (not LLM-judge) for both benign-task utility and attack success
Holding injection content fixed, GPT-5.4 follows an unsafe instruction in README/TODO 2.6x more than in code/data files; full ASR-by-surface tables (Tb.2) and by-position tables reported

Ablation: LLM-based placement selector does not reliably beat a simple frequency-based prior; RL-trained placement-aware attacker (2-stage GRPO) improves attack success over content-only optimization, with transfer tested to a more robust model
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Systematic, multi-agent, multi-domain characterization with deterministic verifiers and ablations; first systematic study of injection *placement* (prior work only varied content or looked at single-surface placement)
reproducibilityEvidence: No explicit code/testbed release statement located in the sections read; paper does note responsible-disclosure framing for the attacker artifacts
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Strong institutional backing, deterministic evaluation, consistent effect across 8 agents and 3 independently-sourced testbeds
candidates.primaryLimitation: Measures conditional ASR among successfully-delivered injections in 3 constructed testbeds; how far the surface-trust ranking (README > code file, etc.) transfers to arbitrary production agent deployments is not tested
candidates.presentationReason: Threat model, testbed construction, and placement-space formalization are all precisely defined with full numeric tables
candidates.reason: Selected: first systematic characterization of indirect-prompt-injection placement (not just content), with a concrete, actionable finding (agents over-trust docs/README-type surfaces) that directly informs defense design.

candidates.title: PCM: A Proof-Carrying Message Protocol for Verifiable Multi-Agent Communication
candidates.citationVelocity: published 2 days; Semantic Scholar 429 rate-limited on 2 retries, not individually confirmed but recency makes 0 citations near-certain
communitySignals: Open-source reference implementation Cygnux-Labs/PCM-protocol (MIT license) with linked Cygnux-Labs/Tracekit signer project
no HF Daily Papers / Papers with Code entry located
credibilityEvidence: Full text read: formal threat model (6 parties, explicit adversary capabilities/non-capabilities), 4 claim types, typed caveat algebra for grant chains, 5 stated security properties with proofs (Sec.9), determinism-by-construction methodology (Sec.10) with 187 conformance vectors
PCM-Lies benchmark: 926 messages from real signer runs (real pytest suites, HTTP fetches, file writes, human approvals), 712 ground-truth-labeled lies across 16 classes

PCM accepts 10/712 lies (1.4%, 95% CI 0.8-2.6%), all stale-evidence class; plain A2A accepts all 712; 6 modeled deployed protocols (A2A signed cards, uAgents, RFC 9421, SCITT, AP2, Verifiable Intent) accept 504-712; two independently-written verifiers agree on all 926 verdicts
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Combines formal security proofs under explicit assumptions with an empirical ground-truth benchmark comparing against 6 real deployed-protocol baselines; author is explicit and precise about non-goals (does not make a compromised agent honest, trusts the signer as TCB, claims are about the past not the present)
reproducibilityEvidence: Specification, JSON Schemas, frozen tool registry, 187 conformance vectors, independent standalone verifier, reference implementation (Tracekit 1.5.0) and benchmark, all MIT-licensed on GitHub
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Narrow, precisely-scoped claim (a signer-backed evidence protocol reduces acceptance of inter-agent lies vs. existing protocols) is directly supported by the benchmark; limitations are stated as precisely as the contributions
candidates.primaryLimitation: Single-author work with no peer review yet; the signer is the trusted computing base, so the approach's real-world value depends on deployments actually isolating signer trust from agent trust, which the benchmark does not test end-to-end in production
candidates.presentationReason: Threat model, protocol mechanics, security properties and evaluation are laid out with explicit formalism and a worked example
candidates.reason: Selected: directly addresses a gap current agent protocols (A2A, MCP) leave open -- receivers have no way to check a sender agent's claims -- with a concrete cryptographic mechanism and head-to-head benchmark against 6 deployed protocols.
